That's imparfait! Use passé composé: j'ai voulu (I wanted).

title: Module 115: être Verbs - DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP (went, came, left)
description: Learn motion verbs that use 'être' in passé composé: je suis allé (I went), je suis venu (I came), je suis parti (I left), je suis arrivé (I arrived)

concepts.term: DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP - Mnemonic for être verbs
concepts.definition: Motion and state-change verbs use ÊTRE (not avoir) in passé composé
concepts.example: je suis allé (I went - with être!), NOT j'ai allé ❌

concepts.definition: Use present tense of être + past participle
concepts.example: je suis allé, tu es venu, il est parti, elle est arrivée

concepts.definition: Descendre, Revenir, Mourir, Retourner, Sortir, Venir, Aller, Naître, Devenir, Entrer, Rentrer, Tomber, Rester, Arriver, Monter, Partir
concepts.example: All motion/state-change verbs - use ÊTRE!

concepts.definition: aller (went), venir (came), partir (left), arriver (arrived), sortir (went out), entrer (entered), rentrer (returned home)
concepts.example: Je suis allé au café, Je suis venu hier, Je suis parti tôt

concepts.definition: Past participle agrees with subject when using être (add e/s/es)
concepts.example: Il est allé (masculine), Elle est allée (+ e for feminine)

concepts.definition: Place ne and pas around être (like with avoir)
concepts.example: Je ne suis pas allé (I didn't go), Elle n'est pas venue (She didn't come)

vocabularyReference.english: I returned home / I came back
I went down / I got off

exercises.prompt: Complete: Hier, je ___ au café (Yesterday, I went to the café) - Use 'aller' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Aller uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'je suis allé' (motion verb).
The past participle is 'allé' (with é): je suis allé, not 'aller'.
That's present/future! Use passé composé: je suis allé (I went).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Tu ___ hier? (Did you come yesterday?) - Use 'venir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Venir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'tu es venu' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: tu es venu (you came).
The past participle is 'venu': tu es venu, not 'es venir'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il ___ tôt (He left early) - Use 'partir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Partir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'il est parti' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: il est parti (he left).
The past participle is 'parti': il est parti, not 'est partir'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ hier soir (We arrived last night) - Use 'arriver' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Arriver uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'nous sommes arrivés' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: nous sommes arrivés.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Vous ___ hier? (Did you go out yesterday?) - Use 'sortir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Sortir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'vous êtes sortis' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: vous êtes sortis.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elles ___ dans le café (They entered the café) - Use 'entrer' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Entrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'elles sont entrées' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: elles sont entrées.

exercises.prompt: Complete: On ___ tard (We came home late / We returned late) - Use 'rentrer' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Rentrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'on est rentré' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: on est rentré (we came home).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ à la maison (I stayed at home) - Use 'rester' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Rester uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'je suis resté' (state verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: je suis resté (I stayed).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Tu ___ dans le bus (You got on the bus / You went up into the bus) - Use 'monter' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Monter uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'tu es monté' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: tu es monté (you got on).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elle ___ du train (She got off the train) - Use 'descendre' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Descendre uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'elle est descendue' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: elle est descendue.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ (I fell) - Use 'tomber' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Tomber uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'je suis tombé' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: je suis tombé (I fell).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il ___ professeur (He became a teacher) - Use 'devenir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Devenir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'il est devenu' (state-change verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: il est devenu (he became).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ne ___ pas ___ (I didn't go) - Use 'aller' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Aller uses ÊTRE! Use 'je ne suis pas allé', not 'ai pas allé'.
That's present tense! Use passé composé: je ne suis pas allé.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ en France (We went to France) - Use 'aller' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Aller uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'nous sommes allés' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: nous sommes allés (we went).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ils ___ hier (They came yesterday) - Use 'venir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Venir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'ils sont venus' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: ils sont venus (they came).

exercises.prompt: Complete: ___ vous ___ en vacances? (Did you go on vacation?) - Use 'partir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Partir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'êtes-vous partis?' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: êtes-vous partis?

exercises.prompt: Complete: On ___ à 8h (We arrived at 8 o'clock) - Use 'arriver' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Arriver uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use 'on est arrivé' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: on est arrivé (we arrived).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elle ne ___ pas ___ (She didn't come) - Use 'venir' with ÊTRE!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Venir uses ÊTRE! Use 'elle n'est pas venue', not 'a pas venu'.
That's present tense! Use passé composé: elle n'est pas venue.

title: Module 116: Past Participle Agreement with être
description: Learn agreement rules: il est allé (he went) vs elle est allée (she went - add e), ils sont allés (they went - add s) vs elles sont allées (add es)

concepts.definition: When using ÊTRE in passé composé, past participle MUST agree with subject in gender and number
concepts.example: il est allé (masculine), elle est allée (+e), ils sont allés (+s), elles sont allées (+es)

concepts.definition: Il/On: No change to past participle (base form)
concepts.example: il est allé, il est venu, il est parti, on est resté

concepts.definition: Elle: Add -e to past participle
concepts.example: elle est allée, elle est venue, elle est partie, elle est restée

concepts.definition: Ils/Nous/Vous (masculine): Add -s to past participle
concepts.example: ils sont allés, nous sommes venus, vous êtes partis

concepts.definition: Elles/Nous/Vous (feminine): Add -es to past participle
concepts.example: elles sont allées, nous sommes venues (all feminine), vous êtes parties (all feminine)

concepts.definition: When group has both masculine and feminine, use masculine plural (-s)
concepts.example: Pierre et Marie sont allés (masculine plural wins)

concepts.definition: This rule ONLY applies to être verbs (DR MRS VANDERTRAMP + reflexives)
concepts.example: j'ai mangé (no change with avoir!), BUT je suis allé/allée (agrees with être)

vocabularyReference.example: Pierre et moi, nous sommes allés
Les garçons, vous êtes allés où?
Les filles, vous êtes allées où?

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elle ___ au café (She went to the café) - Add agreement!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Elle is feminine! Add -e for feminine singular: elle est allée.
That's plural! Elle is singular: elle est allée (just add -e).
Aller uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'elle est allée', not 'a allée'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ils ___ hier (They went yesterday) - Masculine plural agreement!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ils is plural! Add -s for masculine plural: ils sont allés.
That's feminine plural! Use masculine -s for 'ils': ils sont allés.
Aller uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'ils sont allés', not 'ont allés'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Mes sœurs ___ à Paris (My sisters went to Paris) - Feminine plural agreement!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Sœurs (sisters) is feminine! Add -es for feminine plural: sont allées.
Sœurs is plural! Add -es for feminine plural: sont allées.
Aller uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'sont allées', not 'ont allées'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Marie ___ hier (Marie came yesterday) - Use 'venir' with agreement!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Marie is feminine! Add -e for feminine: Marie est venue.
That's plural! Marie is singular: est venue (just -e).
Venir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'est venue', not 'a venue'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ tôt (We left early) - Mixed group (Pierre et moi), use masculine!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Nous is plural! Add -s for masculine plural: sommes partis.
Mixed group uses masculine! Use -s (not -es): sommes partis.
Partir uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'sommes partis', not 'avons partis'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Les filles ___ hier soir (The girls arrived last night) - Feminine plural!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Filles (girls) is feminine! Add -es for feminine plural: sont arrivées.
Les filles is plural! Add -es for feminine plural: sont arrivées.
Arriver uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'sont arrivées', not 'ont arrivées'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Mon frère ___ en France (My brother went to France) - Masculine singular!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Frère (brother) is masculine! No -e needed: mon frère est allé.
Mon frère is singular! No -s needed: est allé (base form).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Vous ___ où, Madame? (Where did you go, Madam?) - Formal singular feminine!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Madame is feminine! Add -e for feminine: vous êtes allée.
Addressing one person! Use singular -e (not plural -es): êtes allée.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Pierre et Marie ___ ensemble (Pierre and Marie left together) - Mixed group!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Mixed group (boy + girl) uses masculine! Use -s: sont partis.
Two people = plural! Add -s for plural: sont partis.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ma mère ___ au marché (My mother went to the market) - Feminine singular!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Mère (mother) is feminine! Add -e for feminine: ma mère est allée.
Ma mère is singular! Just add -e (not plural -es): est allée.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Les garçons ___ tard (The boys came home late) - Use 'rentrer', masculine plural!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Les garçons is plural! Add -s for masculine plural: sont rentrés.
Garçons (boys) is masculine! Use -s (not -es): sont rentrés.
Rentrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's 'sont rentrés', not 'ont rentrés'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ à la maison (We stayed at home) - All girls (Marie et moi), feminine plural!

wrongAnswers.feedback: All girls = feminine plural! Add -es (not -s): sommes restées.
Nous is plural! Add -es for feminine plural: sommes restées.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elle ___ dans le bus (She got on the bus) - Use 'monter', feminine!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Elle is feminine! Add -e for feminine: elle est montée.
That's plural masculine! Elle is singular feminine: est montée.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ils ___ à 8h (They arrived at 8) - Masculine plural!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ils is plural! Add -s for masculine plural: sont arrivés.
Ils is masculine! Use -s (not feminine -es): sont arrivés.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elles ___ hier (They fell yesterday) - Use 'tomber', feminine plural!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Elles is feminine! Add -es for feminine plural: sont tombées.
Elles is plural! Add -es for feminine plural: sont tombées.

exercises.prompt: Complete: On ___ ensemble (We went out together) - Use 'sortir', 'on' = masculine singular!

wrongAnswers.feedback: On is grammatically singular! Use base form: on est sorti (no -s).
On is grammatically masculine! Use base form: on est sorti (no -e).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Vous ___ où, les filles? (Where did you go, girls?) - Plural feminine!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Les filles (girls) is feminine! Add -es for feminine plural: êtes allées.
Les filles is plural! Add -es for plural feminine: êtes allées.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ton ami ___ hier? (Did your friend come yesterday?) - Masculine singular!

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ami (friend - male) is masculine! No -e: ton ami est venu.
Ton ami is singular! Use base form: est venu (no -s).

title: Module 117: Imparfait Formation - All Verbs (was doing, used to do)
description: Learn to form imparfait for ALL verbs using the 'nous stem' rule: je parlais (I was speaking/used to speak), il faisait beau (it was nice), on allait (we used to go)

concepts.term: The Golden Rule: nous stem + -ais endings
concepts.definition: Take 'nous' form of present tense, remove -ons, add -ais endings to ALL verbs (except être)
concepts.example: parler: nous parlons → parl- → je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait

concepts.definition: Take the present tense 'nous' form of the verb
concepts.example: parler → nous parlons, faire → nous faisons, aller → nous allons

concepts.definition: Drop the -ons ending to get the stem
concepts.example: nous parlons → parl-, nous faisons → fais-, nous allons → all-

concepts.definition: Add: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient (same for ALL verbs!)
concepts.example: parl- → je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait, nous parlions, vous parliez, ils parlaient

concepts.definition: être is irregular: ét- stem (not nous sommes) → j'étais, tu étais...
concepts.example: j'étais, tu étais, il était, nous étions, vous étiez, ils étaient

concepts.definition: Descriptions, habits/repeated actions, ongoing states in past, background/scene-setting
concepts.example: Il faisait beau (it was nice - description), Je parlais français tous les jours (I spoke French every day - habit)

vocabularyReference.english: I was speaking / I used to speak
we were going / we used to go
I was taking / I used to take

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ français tous les jours (I used to speak French every day) - Use 'parler' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: je parlais (I used to speak).
That's present tense! Use imparfait: je parlais (I was speaking/used to speak).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'je' form: je parlais (not parlions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il ___ beau (It was nice [weather]) - Use 'faire' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for description: il faisait beau.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: il faisait (it was).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'il' form: il faisait (not faisions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: On ___ au café chaque samedi (We used to go to the café every Saturday) - Use 'aller' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: on allait (we used to go).
That's present tense! Use imparfait: on allait (we used to go).
On uses il/elle form! Use 'on allait', not 'allions' (which is nous).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ partir (I wanted to leave) - Use 'vouloir' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for ongoing desire: je voulais.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: je voulais (I wanted).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'je' form: je voulais (not voulions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il y ___ beaucoup de gens (There were many people) - Use 'avoir' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for description: il y avait.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: il y avait (there were).
'Il y a' uses singular form! Use 'il y avait', not 'avions'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ le bus tous les jours (I used to take the bus every day) - Use 'prendre' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: je prenais.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: je prenais (I used to take).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'je' form: je prenais (not prenions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ contents (We were happy) - Use 'être' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for state: nous étions.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: nous étions (we were).
That's 'je' form! Use 'nous' form: nous étions (not étais).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Tu ___ où? (Where were you? / Where did you use to live?) - Use 'être' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for state: tu étais où?
That's present tense! Use imparfait: tu étais (you were).
That's il/elle form! Use 'tu' form: tu étais (not était).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elle ___ français à l'école (She used to study French at school) - Use 'étudier' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: elle étudiait.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: elle étudiait (she used to study).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'elle' form: elle étudiait (not étudiions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ils ___ au parc (They used to go to the park / They were going to the park) - Use 'aller' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: ils allaient.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: ils allaient (they used to go).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'ils' form: ils allaient (not allions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Vous ___ du café? (Did you want coffee? / Were you wanting coffee?) - Use 'vouloir' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for ongoing state: vous vouliez.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: vous vouliez (you wanted).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'vous' form: vous vouliez (not voulions).

exercises.prompt: Complete: On ___ nos devoirs chaque soir (We used to do our homework each evening) - Use 'faire' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: on faisait.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: on faisait (we used to do).
On uses il/elle form! Use 'on faisait', not 'faisions'.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ au café quand tu m'as appelé (I was going to the café when you called me) - Use 'aller' in imparfait

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for ongoing action: j'allais.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: j'allais (I was going).
That's 'nous' form! Use 'je' form: j'allais (not allions).

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for ongoing past state: ils habitaient.

That's 'nous' form! Use 'ils' form: ils habitaient (not habitions).

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for habits: elle travaillait.

wrongAnswers.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for description: j'étais jeune.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: j'étais (I was).
That's il/elle form! Use 'je' form: j'étais (not était).

That's present tense! Use imparfait: tu étais (you were).

title: Module 118: Passé Composé vs Imparfait - The Golden Rule
description: Learn when to use each past tense: Passé composé for specific events (J'ai mangé - I ate), Imparfait for descriptions/habits (Il faisait beau - It was nice, Je mangeais tous les jours - I used to eat every day)

concepts.definition: PASSÉ COMPOSÉ = Specific completed action (What happened?). IMPARFAIT = Ongoing state/description/habit (How things were/used to be)
concepts.example: J'ai mangé (I ate - specific event) vs Je mangeais (I was eating/used to eat - ongoing or habit)

concepts.definition: Completed actions, countable events, things that started/stopped, main storyline
concepts.example: J'ai vu Marie (I saw Marie - one time), Je suis allé au café (I went to the café - completed)

concepts.definition: Descriptions, ongoing states, repeated habits ('used to'), scene-setting, background information
concepts.example: Il faisait beau (It was nice - description), Je parlais français tous les jours (I used to speak French every day - habit)

concepts.definition: Use imparfait to set the scene, passé composé for what happened
concepts.example: Il faisait beau (background - IMP) quand je suis arrivé (event - PC) = It was nice when I arrived

concepts.definition: PC: hier (yesterday), soudain (suddenly), à 8h (at 8). IMP: tous les jours (every day), toujours (always), d'habitude (usually)
concepts.example: Hier, j'ai mangé (PC - specific time) vs Je mangeais tous les jours (IMP - habit)

concepts.definition: Use imparfait for ongoing action, passé composé for interruption
concepts.example: Je parlais avec Marie (I was talking - IMP) quand tu as appelé (you called - PC event)

concepts.definition: Physical age/description = IMP. Mental state at moment = can be PC
concepts.example: J'avais 20 ans (I was 20 - IMP description) vs J'ai eu peur (I got scared - PC reaction)

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il ___ beau quand je suis arrivé (It was nice when I arrived) - Choose correct tense for 'faire'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Weather description is background! Use imparfait: il faisait beau.
That's present! Use imparfait for description: il faisait.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Hier, j'___ au café (Yesterday, I went to the café) - Choose correct tense for 'aller'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Hier = specific time! Use passé composé: je suis allé (I went).
That's present! Use passé composé for yesterday: je suis allé.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ français tous les jours (I used to speak French every day) - Choose correct tense for 'parler'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Tous les jours = habit! Use imparfait: je parlais (I used to speak).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: je parlais.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ avec Marie quand tu as appelé (I was talking with Marie when you called) - Choose correct tense for 'parler'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ongoing action interrupted! Use imparfait: je parlais (I was talking).
That's present! Use imparfait for ongoing past: je parlais.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Soudain, j'___ Marie (Suddenly, I saw Marie) - Choose correct tense for 'voir'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Soudain = sudden event! Use passé composé: j'ai vu (I saw).
That's present! Use passé composé for past event: j'ai vu.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Quand j'étais jeune, je ___ au foot (When I was young, I used to play soccer) - Choose correct tense for 'jouer'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Repeated past action (habit)! Use imparfait: je jouais (I used to play).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: je jouais.

exercises.prompt: Complete: J'___ content hier (I was happy yesterday) - Choose correct tense for 'être'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Both work! But 'étais' is more natural for ongoing state that day.
That's present! Use imparfait: j'étais content (I was happy).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il y ___ beaucoup de gens (There were many people) - Choose correct tense for 'avoir'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Description of scene! Use imparfait: il y avait (there were).
That's present! Use imparfait for description: il y avait.

exercises.prompt: Complete: À 8h, j'___ (At 8 o'clock, I ate) - Choose correct tense for 'manger'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Specific time (at 8h) = specific event! Use passé composé: j'ai mangé.
That's present! Use passé composé for past event: j'ai mangé.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Pendant que je ___, tu as appelé (While I was eating, you called) - Choose correct tense for 'manger'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ongoing action (while)! Use imparfait: je mangeais (I was eating).
That's present! Use imparfait for ongoing past: je mangeais.

exercises.prompt: Complete: D'habitude, on ___ au café (Usually, we used to go to the café) - Choose correct tense for 'aller'

wrongAnswers.feedback: D'habitude = habit! Use imparfait: on allait (we used to go).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: on allait.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ce jour-là, j'___ malade (That day, I got sick) - Choose correct tense for 'tomber' (tomber malade = get sick)

wrongAnswers.feedback: Getting sick is an event! Use passé composé: je suis tombé malade.
That's present! Use passé composé for past event: je suis tombé.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ils ___ dans un grand appartement (They used to live in a big apartment) - Choose correct tense for 'habiter'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ongoing past state! Use imparfait: ils habitaient (they used to live).
That's present! Use imparfait for past state: ils habitaient.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ le bus tous les matins (I used to take the bus every morning) - Choose correct tense for 'prendre'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Tous les matins = habit! Use imparfait: je prenais (I used to take).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: je prenais.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Hier matin, j'___ le bus (Yesterday morning, I took the bus) - Choose correct tense for 'prendre'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Hier matin = specific time! Use passé composé: j'ai pris (I took).
That's present! Use passé composé for yesterday: j'ai pris.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Elle ___ toujours en retard (She was always late) - Choose correct tense for 'être'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Toujours = repeated state! Use imparfait: elle était toujours en retard.
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: elle était.

exercises.prompt: Complete: À ce moment-là, j'___ (At that moment, I understood) - Choose correct tense for 'comprendre'

wrongAnswers.feedback: À ce moment-là = specific moment! Use passé composé: j'ai compris.
That's present! Use passé composé for past event: j'ai compris.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il ___ du café quand je suis arrivé (He was drinking coffee when I arrived) - Choose correct tense for 'boire'

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ongoing action (was drinking)! Use imparfait: il buvait.
That's present! Use imparfait for ongoing past: il buvait.

title: Module 119: Past Tense Composition - Building Complete Stories
description: Practice combining everything: passé composé, imparfait, causal words, spatial prepositions for rich storytelling

concepts.definition: Combine: 1) Scene-setting (IMP), 2) Events (PC), 3) Causal reasoning (parce que, car), 4) Spatial context (près de, devant)
concepts.example: Hier, il faisait beau donc je suis allé au parc près de chez moi. J'étais content parce que j'avais du temps libre.

concepts.definition: Background (IMP) → Event (PC) → Reason (parce que) → Next Event (PC)
concepts.example: Il faisait beau (background) quand je suis sorti (event). J'ai décidé d'aller au café (event) parce que j'avais faim (reason).

concepts.definition: Use spatial prepositions + imparfait to paint the picture
concepts.example: Le café était près de l'école. Il y avait beaucoup de gens. Ils étaient assis autour des tables.

concepts.definition: Use donc, parce que, car, comme to connect events logically
concepts.example: Comme il faisait beau, je suis sorti. J'ai vu Marie donc on a parlé. On est allés au café car on avait soif.

concepts.definition: Combine temporal words (d'abord, ensuite) with spatial (près de, devant)
concepts.example: D'abord, je suis allé au café près de l'école. Ensuite, j'ai vu Marie devant le cinéma.

exercises.prompt: Complete the story: Hier, il ___ beau ___ je suis sorti (Yesterday, it was nice so I went out) - Use 'faire' + connector

wrongAnswers.feedback: Weather is background! Use imparfait: il faisait (not a fait).
Use 'donc' for result/consequence! Il faisait beau DONC je suis sorti.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je suis allé au café ___ l'école ___ j'avais faim (I went to the café near the school because I was hungry) - Spatial + causal

wrongAnswers.feedback: Close! But 'près de' (near) is better than 'devant' (in front) here.
The café is NEAR the school, not IN it! Use 'près de' (near).

exercises.prompt: Complete: J'___ avec Marie quand tu as appelé (I was talking with Marie when you called) - Use 'parler' in correct tense

wrongAnswers.feedback: Actually BOTH work! But if thinking of whole conversation as one unit, 'ai parlé' works. If emphasizing ongoing, 'parlais' is better. Let's accept both!

exercises.prompt: Complete: ___ il faisait beau, on est allés au parc (Since it was nice, we went to the park) - Use causal word at START

wrongAnswers.feedback: Parce que rarely starts sentences! Use 'Comme' at the beginning.
Car CANNOT start a sentence! Use 'Comme' at the beginning.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Il y ___ beaucoup de gens ___ des tables (There were many people around the tables) - Description + spatial

wrongAnswers.feedback: Description of scene! Use imparfait: il y avait (not a eu).
People sit AROUND tables, not ON them! Use 'autour de' (around).

exercises.prompt: Complete: C'___ super! (It was great!) - Always use imparfait for 'c'était'

wrongAnswers.feedback: C'était is ALWAYS imparfait for general evaluation! C'était super.
That's present! Use imparfait: c'était (it was).

exercises.prompt: Complete: J'ai décidé ___ aller au cinéma ___ j'avais du temps (I decided to go to the cinema because I had time) - Infinitive + reason

wrongAnswers.feedback: Both work! 'Parce que' or 'car' are both fine for 'because'.
'Décider DE' (not à)! J'ai décidé D'aller (not à aller).

exercises.prompt: Complete: On ___ au café chaque samedi, mais hier on n'y est pas allé (We used to go to the café every Saturday, but yesterday we didn't go) - Habit vs specific

wrongAnswers.feedback: Chaque samedi = habit! Use imparfait: on allait (we used to go).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: on allait.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Je marchais tranquillement quand soudain j'___ Marie (I was walking peacefully when suddenly I saw Marie) - Ongoing + event

wrongAnswers.feedback: Soudain = sudden event! Use passé composé: j'ai vu (I saw).
That's present! Use passé composé for past event: j'ai vu.

exercises.prompt: Complete: ___ j'avais faim, j'ai mangé (Thanks to being hungry, I ate) - WRONG! Fix: ___ j'avais faim, j'ai mangé (Because I was hungry, I ate)

wrongAnswers.feedback: Grâce à is POSITIVE and needs a NOUN! Use 'Parce que' + clause for hunger.
À cause de needs a NOUN! Use 'Parce que j'avais faim' (because I was hungry).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Le livre était ___ la table ___ ma chambre (The book was on the table in my room) - Two spatial prepositions

wrongAnswers.feedback: Wrong order! The book is ON (sur) the table, IN (dans) the room.
Au-dessus means 'above' (hanging). Use 'sur' for 'on' (touching surface).

exercises.prompt: Complete: Pendant que je ___, on a parlé pendant une heure (While I was there, we talked for an hour) - Use 'être' for location

wrongAnswers.feedback: Ongoing state (while there)! Use imparfait: j'étais (I was there).
That's present! Use imparfait for past state: j'étais.

exercises.prompt: Complete: J'___ mes devoirs ___ j'ai regardé la télé (I did my homework then I watched TV) - Two events in sequence

wrongAnswers.feedback: Completed homework = specific event! Use passé composé: j'ai fait.
'Car' is for reason! Use 'ensuite' (then) for sequence.

exercises.prompt: Complete: ___ toi, j'ai réussi (Thanks to you, I succeeded) - Positive attribution

wrongAnswers.feedback: Parce que needs a CLAUSE! Use 'Grâce à toi' (thanks to you - NOUN).
Succeeding is POSITIVE! Use 'grâce à' (not à cause de which is negative/neutral).

exercises.prompt: Complete: ___ la pluie, on est restés à la maison (Because of the rain, we stayed home) - Negative reason + noun

wrongAnswers.feedback: Rain isn't positive! Use 'à cause de' for negative/neutral reasons.
Parce que needs a CLAUSE! Use 'à cause de la pluie' (because of THE RAIN - noun).

readingPassage.title: Un Samedi à Paris
readingPassage.text:
Hier, c'était samedi et il faisait très beau à Paris. J'étais content parce que c'était le week-end et je n'avais pas de travail.

D'abord, je me suis réveillé à 8h. D'habitude, je me levais plus tard le samedi, mais ce jour-là, j'ai voulu sortir tôt parce que le temps était si beau.

Après mon café, je suis allé au Jardin du Luxembourg près de ma maison. J'aime beaucoup ce parc! Il y avait beaucoup de gens dans le jardin. C'était une belle journée.

Je suis allé près du lac quand soudain j'ai vu mon ami Pierre. Il était assis sur un banc sous un grand arbre. Je suis allé vers lui et on a commencé à parler.

"Salut Pierre! Qu'est-ce que tu fais ici?" j'ai demandé.

"Bonjour! Je voulais être dehors parce qu'il faisait si beau. Je suis content que tu sois là!" il a dit.

Nous avons parlé pendant une heure. Il m'a dit qu'il voulait un nouveau travail à la Sorbonne parce qu'il n'aimait pas son travail. Je lui ai dit que je comprenais car j'ai eu le même problème l'année dernière.

Ensuite, comme nous avions faim, nous avons décidé d'aller au Café de Flore qui est en face du jardin. Le Café de Flore est très bon et très célèbre à Paris! Il y avait beaucoup de gens - à côté des fenêtres, autour des tables, partout!

Nous avons commandé des sandwichs et du café. Pendant que nous mangions, nous avons vu Marie. Elle est entrée dans le café. Elle nous a vus et elle est venue à notre table.

"Quelle surprise!" elle a dit. "Je ne savais pas que vous étiez ici!"

Marie était notre amie de la Sorbonne. Nous ne l'avons pas vue depuis six mois parce qu'elle est maintenant à Lyon. Grâce à cette rencontre, nous avons pu être ensemble pour l'après-midi.

L'après-midi, nous sommes allés au cinéma près de la gare. Il y avait le film "Amélie" - un très bon film français! Le cinéma était à dix minutes du Café de Flore.

Le film était excellent! Nous avons beaucoup aimé Amélie. Après le film, nous avons décidé de manger ensemble au Restaurant Le Procope qui est derrière le cinéma. Le Procope est le plus vieux restaurant de Paris!

Au restaurant, nous avons mangé de la bonne cuisine française. C'était délicieux! Nous avons parlé de la Sorbonne, de nos vies, et de ce que nous voulons faire.

À cause du temps, Marie a dû partir vers 9h pour rentrer à Lyon. Pierre et moi sommes restés un peu plus. Nous avons pris un dernier café ensemble.

Finalement, je suis rentré chez moi vers 10h. J'étais fatigué mais très heureux. C'était une journée parfaite à Paris.

Parfois, les meilleures journées sont celles qu'on ne pense pas avoir. Grâce à ma sortie au Jardin du Luxembourg, j'ai eu une très belle journée avec mes amis.

Avant de dormir, j'ai pensé: "C'est pour ça que j'aime les samedis à Paris!"
readingPassage.translation:
Yesterday, it was Saturday and the weather was very nice in Paris. I was happy because it was the weekend and I had no work.

First, I woke up at 8am. Usually, I used to get up later on Saturdays, but that day, I wanted to go out early because the weather was so nice.

After my coffee, I went to Jardin du Luxembourg near my house. I really like this park! There were many people in the garden. It was a beautiful day.

I went near the lake when suddenly I saw my friend Pierre. He was sitting on a bench under a big tree. I went towards him and we started talking.

"Hi Pierre! What are you doing here?" I asked.

"Hello! I wanted to be outside because it was so nice. I'm glad you're here!" he said.

We talked for an hour. He told me he wanted a new job at the Sorbonne because he didn't like his job. I told him that I understood because I had the same problem last year.

Then, since we were hungry, we decided to go to Café de Flore which is across from the garden. Café de Flore is very good and very famous in Paris! There were many people - next to the windows, around the tables, everywhere!

We ordered sandwiches and coffee. While we were eating, we saw Marie. She entered the café. She saw us and she came to our table.

"What a surprise!" she said. "I didn't know you were here!"

Marie was our friend from the Sorbonne. We haven't seen her for six months because she's now in Lyon. Thanks to this meeting, we were able to be together for the afternoon.

In the afternoon, we went to the cinema near the station. There was the film "Amélie" - a very good French film! The cinema was ten minutes from Café de Flore.

The film was excellent! We really liked Amélie. After the film, we decided to eat together at Restaurant Le Procope which is behind the cinema. Le Procope is the oldest restaurant in Paris!

At the restaurant, we ate good French food. It was delicious! We talked about the Sorbonne, about our lives, and about what we want to do.

Because of the time, Marie had to leave around 9pm to go back to Lyon. Pierre and I stayed a bit longer. We had one last coffee together.

Finally, I went home around 10pm. I was tired but very happy. It was a perfect day in Paris.

Sometimes, the best days are the ones we don't think we'll have. Thanks to my outing to Jardin du Luxembourg, I had a very beautiful day with my friends.

Before sleeping, I thought: "That's why I love Saturdays in Paris!"

title: Module 123: Forms Used After 'il faut que' and 'je veux que'
description: Learn verb forms that appear after 'il faut que...' and 'je veux que...' phrases. sois (be), ait (have), aille (go), fasse (do). Essential for telling people what you want them to do!

concepts.definition: French uses different verb forms after phrases like 'il faut que' (someone needs to), 'je veux que' (I want someone to), 'je suis content que' (I'm happy that someone...). These express wishes, needs, or emotions about OTHER PEOPLE's actions.
concepts.example: Normal statement: Tu es sage (You are good). Wish about you: Il faut que tu sois sage (You need to be good - different form!)

concepts.term: Where You CAN Use These Forms
concepts.definition: ONLY after certain phrases: il faut que, je veux que, je suis content que, j'ai peur que, avant que, pour que, bien que, etc.
concepts.example: ✓ Il faut que tu sois sage (You need to be good), ✓ Je veux qu'il aille (I want him to go)

concepts.term: Where You CANNOT Use These Forms
concepts.definition: DON'T use these for normal statements, questions, or with just il faut/je veux (no 'que')
concepts.example: ✗ Tu sois content? (Wrong! Say: Tu es content?). ✗ Il faut aller (Correct - no 'que' = normal form)

concepts.definition: If you see 'que' + a person after these starter phrases, use these forms!
concepts.example: il faut QUE tu → use sois/aies/ailles/fasses, je veux QUE tu → use sois/aies/ailles/fasses

title: Module 124: More Forms for 'il faut que' and 'je veux que' Phrases
description: More verb forms that appear after 'il faut que...' and 'je veux que...' phrases. vienne (come), parte (leave), puisse (can), sache (know), comprenne (understand). Essential for wishes and commands!

concepts.definition: Like the previous special forms module, these verbs change ONLY after phrases with 'que' (il faut que, je veux que, je suis content que, etc.)
concepts.example: Normal: tu viens (you come) → After 'je veux que': tu viennes. Normal: tu peux (you can) → After 'il faut que': tu puisses

concepts.term: When To Use vs When NOT To Use
concepts.definition: USE: After 'que' in wish/need/emotion phrases. DON'T USE: For normal statements or questions.
concepts.example: ✓ Je veux que tu viennes (I want you to come). ✗ Tu viennes ici? (Wrong! Say: Tu viens ici?)

concepts.definition: If you see 'il faut/je veux/je suis content + QUE + person', use these forms. No 'que' = normal forms.
concepts.example: Il faut partir (leave - normal). Il faut QUE tu partes (you leave - changed form!)

readingPassage.title: Un Rêve à Paris
readingPassage.text:
Je m'appelle Sophie et j'habite à Paris depuis cinq ans. J'adore cette ville! Mais j'ai toujours un grand rêve: je veux que ma vie soit différente.

Hier soir, j'étais assise dans un petit café près de Notre-Dame. Je regardais la belle cathédrale et je pensais à mes rêves. Il faisait froid mais j'étais contente d'être là.

J'avais déjà fini mon travail pour la journée. J'avais déjà pensé à beaucoup de choses. Maintenant, je voulais simplement rêver un peu.

Si j'étais riche, j'achèterais une petite maison à Montmartre. J'aimerais habiter dans ce quartier célèbre où les artistes ont vécu. Si j'avais plus d'argent, je voyagerais aussi à Nice et à Bordeaux.

Mon ami Marc est arrivé au café. Il savait que j'aime ce café parce que c'est près de Notre-Dame. Je suis contente qu'il soit venu! On se parle toujours de nos rêves.

"Salut Sophie! Je savais que tu serais ici," il a dit.

"Bonjour Marc! Je suis heureuse que tu sois là. J'étais en train de penser à mes rêves," j'ai dit.

"Ah oui? Moi aussi, j'ai beaucoup de rêves. Je veux que ma vie change," il a dit.

Marc m'a dit qu'il voulait être artiste. Il voulait que les gens voient ses peintures au Louvre un jour. C'est un grand rêve! Le Louvre est le musée le plus célèbre du monde.

"Je veux qu'un jour mes peintures soient au Louvre. Mais j'ai peur que ce soit difficile," il a dit.

"Je comprends. Mais il faut que tu essaies! Si tu ne fais rien, tu ne sauras jamais," j'ai dit.

Nous avons parlé pendant une heure. Je lui ai dit que je voulais être professeur de français. J'aimerais que mes étudiants adorent la langue française comme moi.

"Je suis content que tu aies ce rêve. Tu serais une excellente professeur," Marc a dit.

"Merci! Mais j'ai peur que ce soit trop difficile. J'avais déjà essayé l'année dernière mais je n'ai pas réussi," j'ai dit.

"Il faut que tu essaies encore! Si j'étais toi, je ne renoncerais pas," il a dit.

Marc avait raison. Avant que nous parlions, j'avais déjà perdu espoir. Mais maintenant, je me sens mieux.

Nous avons décidé d'aider l'un l'autre. Je veux qu'il réussisse avec ses peintures, et il veut que je réussisse comme professeur.

"Je suis heureux que nous soyons amis. On peut s'aider," Marc a dit.

"Moi aussi! J'aimerais que nous réussissions tous les deux," j'ai dit.

Après notre café, nous avons marché vers la Seine. Il faisait nuit maintenant et Paris était magnifique. Les lumières de la Tour Eiffel brillaient au loin.

"Si on avait plus de temps, on pourrait marcher toute la nuit," Marc a dit.

"Oui ! J'adore Paris la nuit. C'est pour ça que je veux rester ici toute ma vie," j'ai dit.

Nous nous sommes dit au revoir près du pont. Avant de partir, Marc m'a dit quelque chose d'important.

"Sophie, il faut que tu saches une chose: tes rêves sont importants. Je veux que tu continues à essayer," il a dit.

"Merci Marc. Je suis reconnaissante que tu m'aies dit ça. Toi aussi, tu dois continuer avec tes peintures," j'ai dit.

En rentrant chez moi, j'ai pensé à notre conversation. Je regrette que j'aie perdu espoir avant. Mais maintenant, je suis contente que Marc soit mon ami.

Si j'avais su plus tôt que l'espoir était si important, j'aurais continué mes études. Mais il n'est pas trop tard!

Demain, je vais appeler l'université. Il faut que je demande des informations pour devenir professeur. Je veux que mes rêves deviennent réalité.

Grâce à mon ami et à cette belle soirée à Paris, j'ai retrouvé mon courage. Je suis heureuse que cette ville existe, et je suis contente que mes amis me soutiennent.

Comme Marc a dit: il faut essayer! Si on ne fait rien, on ne saura jamais. Et moi, je veux savoir si mes rêves peuvent devenir réalité.
readingPassage.translation:
My name is Sophie and I've been living in Paris for five years. I love this city! But I always have a big dream: I want my life to be different.

Last night, I was sitting in a small café near Notre-Dame. I was looking at the beautiful cathedral and thinking about my dreams. It was cold but I was happy to be there.

I had already finished my work for the day. I had already thought about many things. Now, I just wanted to dream a little.

If I were rich, I'd buy a small house in Montmartre. I'd like to live in this famous neighborhood where artists have lived. If I had more money, I'd also travel to Nice and Bordeaux.

My friend Marc arrived at the café. He knew I like this café because it's near Notre-Dame. I'm glad he came! We always talk to each other about our dreams.

"Hi Sophie! I knew you'd be here," he said.

"Hello Marc! I'm happy you're here. I was thinking about my dreams," I said.

"Oh yes? Me too, I have many dreams. I want my life to change," he said.

Marc told me he wanted to be an artist. He wanted people to see his paintings at the Louvre one day. It's a big dream! The Louvre is the most famous museum in the world.

"I want my paintings to be at the Louvre one day. But I'm afraid it might be difficult," he said.

"I understand. But you have to try! If you don't do anything, you'll never know," I said.

We talked for an hour. I told him I wanted to be a French teacher. I'd like my students to love the French language like me.

"I'm glad you have this dream. You'd be an excellent teacher," Marc said.

"Thank you! But I'm afraid it might be too difficult. I had already tried last year but I didn't succeed," I said.

"You have to try again! If I were you, I wouldn't give up," he said.

Marc was right. Before we talked, I had already lost hope. But now, I feel better.

We decided to help each other. I want him to succeed with his paintings, and he wants me to succeed as a teacher.

"I'm happy we're friends. We can help each other," Marc said.

"Me too! I'd like us both to succeed," I said.

After our coffee, we walked towards the Seine. It was night now and Paris was magnificent. The lights of the Eiffel Tower were shining in the distance.

"If we had more time, we could walk all night," Marc said.

"Yes! I love Paris at night. That's why I want to stay here all my life," I said.

We said goodbye near the bridge. Before leaving, Marc told me something important.

"Sophie, you need to know one thing: your dreams are important. I want you to keep trying," he said.

"Thank you Marc. I'm grateful you told me that. You too, you must continue with your paintings," I said.

Walking home, I thought about our conversation. I regret that I lost hope before. But now, I'm glad Marc is my friend.

If I had known earlier that hope was so important, I would have continued my studies. But it's not too late!

Tomorrow, I'm going to call the university. I need to ask for information to become a teacher. I want my dreams to become reality.

Thanks to my friend and to this beautiful evening in Paris, I found my courage again. I'm happy this city exists, and I'm glad my friends support me.

Like Marc said: you have to try! If we don't do anything, we'll never know. And me, I want to know if my dreams can become reality.

readingPassage.title: La France d'Aujourd'hui : Un Pays en Mouvement
readingPassage.text:
La France d'aujourd'hui est un pays qui continue à évoluer rapidement. Avec ses soixante-huit millions d'habitants, elle reste une nation importante en Europe et dans le monde.

Paris, sa capitale, compte plus de deux millions de personnes. Cette ville magnifique attire des millions de visiteurs chaque année. Ils viennent admirer ses monuments célèbres comme la Tour Eiffel, Notre-Dame, le Louvre, et l'Arc de Triomphe sur les Champs-Élysées. Beaucoup visitent aussi le château de Versailles. Les touristes cherchent souvent des directions pour trouver ces lieux historiques.

Le système éducatif français est reconnu internationalement. Les étudiants français travaillent dur dans leurs écoles et universités. Ils étudient beaucoup de matières différentes : les sciences, l'histoire, les langues étrangères, et la littérature. L'apprentissage commence très jeune - les enfants ont généralement six ans quand ils arrivent à l'école primaire.

La culture française influence le monde entier. Les artistes français comme Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir, et Vincent van Gogh ont créé des œuvres magnifiques. Ces peintres impressionnistes vivent encore dans la mémoire collective. Aujourd'hui, les nouveaux artistes vivent souvent dans des quartiers comme Montmartre, près du célèbre Moulin Rouge.

La cuisine française reste également très populaire dans le monde. Les plats traditionnels comme le coq au vin, la ratatouille, et la bouillabaisse de Marseille donnent du plaisir à des millions de personnes. Les restaurants français créent des expériences culinaires inoubliables.

L'économie française dépend de plusieurs secteurs importants. Beaucoup de Français travaillent dans les services, d'autres dans l'industrie ou l'agriculture. Les entreprises françaises exportent leurs produits vers l'est, l'ouest, le nord et le sud - dans toute l'Europe et au-delà.

Le transport public fonctionne très bien en France. Les trains rapides connectent les grandes villes comme Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, et Nice. Les voyageurs peuvent arriver rapidement à leur destination. Dans Paris, le métro permet aux habitants de se déplacer facilement. Ils attendent quelques minutes seulement entre les trains.

Les Français adorent leurs vacances. En été, ils voyagent souvent vers le sud pour profiter du soleil et de la mer Méditerranée. Nice et Cannes sont des destinations très populaires. D'autres préfèrent rester dans leur région et découvrir la beauté de la campagne française.

La technologie change aussi la vie quotidienne en France. Les jeunes Français écoutent de la musique en ligne, regardent des films sur internet, et communiquent avec leurs amis via leurs téléphones. Cette génération vit différemment de leurs parents, mais elle garde les valeurs françaises importantes.

Aujourd'hui, la France travaille activement pour protéger l'environnement. Le gouvernement encourage les citoyens à utiliser les transports publics, à recycler leurs déchets, et à économiser l'énergie. Ces efforts montrent que la France pense à l'avenir de la planète.

Les relations internationales restent très importantes pour la France. Elle participe activement aux organisations européennes et mondiales. Les diplomates français voyagent régulièrement pour rencontrer leurs homologues étrangers. Ils discutent de questions économiques, politiques, et culturelles.

En conclusion, la France moderne combine tradition et innovation. Elle préserve son patrimoine historique tout en embrassant les changements du vingt et unième siècle. Cette nation continue à jouer un rôle significatif sur la scène internationale, et ses contributions enrichissent notre monde.
readingPassage.translation:
Modern France is a country that continues to evolve rapidly. With its sixty-eight million inhabitants, it remains an important nation in Europe and in the world.

Paris, its capital, has more than two million people. This magnificent city attracts millions of visitors each year. They come to admire its famous monuments like the Eiffel Tower, Notre-Dame, the Louvre, and the Arc de Triomphe on the Champs-Élysées. Many also visit the Palace of Versailles. Tourists often look for directions to find these historic places.

The French educational system is internationally recognized. French students work hard in their schools and universities. They study many different subjects: sciences, history, foreign languages, and literature. Learning begins very young - children are generally six years old when they arrive at elementary school.

French culture influences the entire world. French artists like Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir, and Vincent van Gogh created magnificent works. These Impressionist painters still live in collective memory. Today, new artists often live in neighborhoods like Montmartre, near the famous Moulin Rouge.

French cuisine also remains very popular worldwide. Traditional dishes like coq au vin, ratatouille, and Marseille's bouillabaisse give pleasure to millions of people. French restaurants create unforgettable culinary experiences.

The French economy depends on several important sectors. Many French people work in services, others in industry or agriculture. French companies export their products to the east, west, north and south - throughout Europe and beyond.

Public transportation works very well in France. Fast trains connect major cities like Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, and Nice. Travelers can arrive quickly at their destination. In Paris, the metro allows inhabitants to move around easily. They wait only a few minutes between trains.

The French love their vacations. In summer, they often travel south to enjoy the sun and the Mediterranean Sea. Nice and Cannes are very popular destinations. Others prefer to stay in their region and discover the beauty of the French countryside.

Technology is also changing daily life in France. Young French people listen to music online, watch movies on the internet, and communicate with their friends via their phones. This generation lives differently from their parents, but keeps important French values.

Today, France works actively to protect the environment. The government encourages citizens to use public transport, to recycle their waste, and to save energy. These efforts show that France thinks about the future of the planet.

International relations remain very important for France. It participates actively in European and global organizations. French diplomats travel regularly to meet their foreign counterparts. They discuss economic, political, and cultural questions.

In conclusion, modern France combines tradition and innovation. It preserves its historic heritage while embracing the changes of the twenty-first century. This nation continues to play a significant role on the international stage, and its contributions enrich our world.

title: Module 155: qu'est-ce qui vs qu'est-ce que - Master 'What' Questions
description: THE BIGGEST distinction in French questions: qu'est-ce qui (what DOES - subject) vs qu'est-ce que (what DO you - object). Master this, ask anything!

concepts.definition: qu'est-ce qui = what DOES something (subject). qu'est-ce que = what DO you verb (object)
concepts.example: Qu'est-ce qui brille? (What shines? - subject) vs Qu'est-ce que tu vois? (What do you see? - object)

concepts.definition: Use QUI when asking WHAT is doing the action. No other subject after qui!
concepts.example: Qu'est-ce qui brille? (What shines?), Qu'est-ce qui fait du bruit? (What makes noise?), Qu'est-ce qui rend l'herbe verte? (What makes grass green?)

concepts.definition: Use QUE when asking what someone/something DOES TO something. Subject comes after que!
concepts.example: Qu'est-ce que tu vois? (What do you see?), Qu'est-ce que tu manges? (What are you eating?), Qu'est-ce que le soleil fait? (What does the sun do?)

concepts.definition: If verb has NO object → use QUI. If verb has an object → use QUE
concepts.example: Pattern: [qu'est-ce qui] + [VERB] OR [qu'est-ce que] + [SUBJECT] + [VERB]

concepts.term: Transform ANY Statement into a Question
concepts.definition: You can now ask 'what' questions about anything you've learned!
concepts.example: Le soleil brille → Qu'est-ce qui brille? (What shines?), Je vois un oiseau → Qu'est-ce que tu vois? (What do you see?)

SUBJECT question - thing is doing the falling
SUBJECT question - thing is making noise
SUBJECT question - thing is making grass green
OBJECT question - you are seeing WHAT
OBJECT question - you are eating WHAT
OBJECT question - birds are eating WHAT

Perfect causative question! But use 'qu'est-ce QUI' because the subject (what) is DOING the action of making grass green.

wrongAnswers.feedback: Use 'qu'est-ce QUE' when asking what you DO to something (object). You see SOMETHING. That something is the object. QUI = subject, QUE = object.
Use 'qu'est-ce QUE' for object questions. You are seeing WHAT - that's the object of your seeing!

title: Module 158: qui est-ce qui vs qui est-ce que - Master 'Who' Questions
description: Same pattern as WHAT questions, but for WHO! qui est-ce qui (who DOES - subject) vs qui est-ce que (who DO you - object). Transfer learning!

concepts.definition: You already know this pattern from the qu'est-ce qui module - just change WHAT to WHO!
concepts.example: qu'est-ce qui → qui est-ce qui (what DOES → who DOES), qu'est-ce que → qui est-ce que (what DO you → who DO you)

concepts.definition: Use QUI when asking WHO is doing the action. No other subject after qui!
concepts.example: Qui est-ce qui parle? (Who speaks?), Qui est-ce qui fait ça? (Who does that?), Qui est-ce qui nage? (Who swims?)

concepts.definition: Use QUE when asking who someone DOES something to. Subject comes after que!
concepts.example: Qui est-ce que tu vois? (Who do you see?), Qui est-ce que tu aimes? (Who do you like?), Qui est-ce que je dois appeler? (Who should I call?)

concepts.term: Transfer Learning from qu'est-ce qui Module
concepts.definition: You mastered qu'est-ce qui/que discrimination - same rule applies here!
concepts.example: Subject (thing doing action) → QUI. Object (thing receiving action) → QUE

title: Module 159: Inversion Questions - Formal Register
description: Master formal French questions with inversion: Pourquoi les nuages sont-ils blancs? Comment fait-on ça? Où vas-tu? Add stylistic range!

concepts.definition: In formal French, flip the verb and subject with a hyphen
concepts.example: Informal: Comment est-ce que tu fais ça? Formal: Comment fais-tu ça?

concepts.definition: More common in: formal writing, literature, professional settings, with question words
concepts.example: Où vas-tu? (Where are you going?), Quand arrives-tu? (When do you arrive?)

concepts.definition: Add -t- between vowel-ending verbs and il/elle/on for pronunciation
concepts.example: a + il → a-t-il (Pourquoi a-t-il ça?), va + elle → va-t-elle (Où va-t-elle?)

concepts.definition: When subject is a noun phrase, keep noun then add inverted pronoun
concepts.example: Les nuages sont-ils blancs? (noun 'les nuages' + inverted 'sont-ils')

concepts.definition: Students can choose based on formality level - both are valid French
concepts.example: Casual: Comment est-ce que tu fais ça? Formal: Comment fais-tu ça? (same meaning)

title: Module 160: Embedded Questions - Polite Indirect Questions
description: Soften questions by embedding them: Je me demande pourquoi c'est comme ça. Je ne sais pas comment on fait ça. Natural conversation flow!

concepts.definition: Embed a question inside a statement to make it softer and more polite
concepts.example: Direct: Pourquoi est-ce que c'est comme ça? Embedded: Je me demande pourquoi c'est comme ça.

concepts.definition: 'Je me demande' (I wonder), 'Je ne sais pas' (I don't know), 'Peux-tu me dire' (Can you tell me)
concepts.example: Je me demande comment..., Je ne sais pas pourquoi..., Peux-tu me dire où...?

concepts.term: NO est-ce que After These Phrases!
concepts.definition: After embedding starters, use statement word order - no est-ce que needed
concepts.example: Je me demande pourquoi le ciel est bleu (NOT: Je me demande pourquoi est-ce que le ciel est bleu)

concepts.definition: Embedded questions sound less direct and more conversational
concepts.example: Direct: Où est la gare? Polite: Peux-tu me dire où est la gare?

concepts.definition: Native speakers use embedded questions constantly in casual speech
concepts.example: Tu sais pourquoi il fait ça? On ne comprend pas comment ça marche.

title: Module 161: Rhetorical & Negative Questions - Advanced Style
description: Add native sophistication: N'est-ce pas vrai? (Isn't that true?), Comment ne pas aimer ça? (How can you not love that?), Qui ne voudrait pas ça? (Who wouldn't want that?)

concepts.definition: Ask negative questions to seek agreement or confirmation
concepts.example: N'est-ce pas vrai? (Isn't that true?), N'as-tu pas faim? (Aren't you hungry?)

concepts.definition: Ask questions that express opinion rather than seeking actual answers
concepts.example: Comment ne pas aimer ça? (How can you not love that? = Of course you love it!), Qui ne voudrait pas ça? (Who wouldn't want that? = Everyone wants it!)

concepts.definition: In negative questions, ne comes before verb, pas after (or before infinitive)
concepts.example: N'es-tu pas content? Ne veux-tu pas essayer? Comment ne pas aimer?

concepts.definition: These questions are tools for persuasive speech and emphasizing points
concepts.example: Pourquoi ne pas essayer? (Why not try? = You should try!)

concepts.definition: Using these questions makes your French sound more sophisticated and natural
concepts.example: From basic: Tu aimes ça? To sophisticated: Comment ne pas aimer ça?

title: Module 162: Multi-Clause Questions - Full Complexity
description: Peak composition! Combine questions with subjunctive/conditional: Pourquoi est-ce que tu veux que je fasse ça? Comment est-ce que tu penses qu'on devrait faire ça?

concepts.definition: Combine question words with all the sophisticated structures from Unit 10
concepts.example: Pourquoi est-ce qu'il faut que je fasse ça? (Why do I have to do that? - necessity + question)

concepts.definition: Ask questions about wishes, emotions, necessity using subjunctive
concepts.example: Comment est-ce que tu veux que je le fasse? (How do you want me to do it?)

concepts.definition: Ask about what people think using penser/croire patterns
concepts.example: Pourquoi est-ce que tu penses que c'est comme ça? (Why do you think it's like that?)

concepts.definition: Ask hypothetical questions using conditional mood
concepts.example: Qu'est-ce qui rendrait l'herbe plus verte? (What would make grass greener?)

concepts.definition: These questions demonstrate complete mastery of French question formation
concepts.example: Can ask ANY question about ANY thought - you've reached full competency!

title: Reference I: L'Alphabet
description: The French alphabet with pronunciation guide - 26 letters with unique French sounds

concepts.definition: French uses the same 26 letters as English, but pronunciation is very different!
concepts.example: A (ah), B (bay), C (say), D (day), E (euh), F (eff), G (zhay), H (ash), I (ee), J (zhee), K (kah), L (ell), M (emm), N (enn), O (oh), P (pay), Q (koo), R (air), S (ess), T (tay), U (oo), V (vay), W (doo-bluh-vay), X (eex), Y (ee-grek), Z (zed)

concepts.definition: The acute accent - appears only on 'e' and makes it sound like 'ay'
concepts.example: café, été (summer), déjà

concepts.definition: The grave accent - on 'e' makes it sound like 'eh', on 'a' and 'u' it distinguishes meaning
concepts.example: très, où (where), là (there)

concepts.term: Accent Circonflexe (â, ê, î, ô, û)
concepts.definition: The circumflex - can appear on any vowel, often indicates a historical 's' was dropped
concepts.example: être (to be), hôtel, pâtes (pasta), île (island)

concepts.definition: The diaeresis - indicates two vowels are pronounced separately
concepts.example: Noël (Christmas), naïve, maïs (corn)

concepts.definition: The cedilla - makes 'c' sound like 's' before a, o, u
concepts.example: ça, français, garçon (boy)

concepts.definition: Two letters merged together - œ is common, æ is rare
concepts.example: cœur (heart), sœur (sister), curriculum vitæ

vocabularyReference.note: feminine - a, e, i, o, u, y

exercises.hint: feminine - a, e, i, o, u, y

title: Reference II: Les Nombres
description: French numbers from 0 to infinity - including the unique 70s, 80s, and 90s!

concepts.definition: The foundation numbers you need to memorize
concepts.example: 0 zéro, 1 un, 2 deux, 3 trois, 4 quatre, 5 cinq, 6 six, 7 sept, 8 huit, 9 neuf, 10 dix, 11 onze, 12 douze, 13 treize, 14 quatorze, 15 quinze, 16 seize, 17 dix-sept, 18 dix-huit, 19 dix-neuf, 20 vingt

concepts.definition: Regular tens that follow a pattern
concepts.example: 20 vingt, 30 trente, 40 quarante, 50 cinquante, 60 soixante

concepts.definition: 70 = sixty-ten (soixante-dix). French counts: 71 (sixty-eleven), 72 (sixty-twelve), etc.
concepts.example: 70 soixante-dix, 71 soixante-et-onze, 75 soixante-quinze, 79 soixante-dix-neuf

concepts.definition: 80 = four-twenties (quatre-vingts). A remnant of Celtic base-20 counting!
concepts.example: 80 quatre-vingts, 81 quatre-vingt-un, 85 quatre-vingt-cinq, 89 quatre-vingt-neuf

concepts.definition: 90 = four-twenty-ten (quatre-vingt-dix). Combining both systems!
concepts.example: 90 quatre-vingt-dix, 91 quatre-vingt-onze, 95 quatre-vingt-quinze, 99 quatre-vingt-dix-neuf

concepts.definition: Add single digits with a hyphen. Use 'et' (and) for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61
concepts.example: 21 vingt-et-un, 22 vingt-deux, 35 trente-cinq, 47 quarante-sept, 69 soixante-neuf

concepts.definition: Hundreds, thousands, millions - building bigger numbers
concepts.example: 100 cent, 200 deux cents, 1000 mille, 1,000,000 un million, 1,000,000,000 un milliard

concepts.definition: More logical! Belgium and Switzerland use: 70 septante, 90 nonante
concepts.example: 70 septante (vs soixante-dix), 90 nonante (vs quatre-vingt-dix). Much easier!

concepts.definition: Key exceptions you need to know to avoid common mistakes
concepts.example: 1) 'et' (and) only for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61, 71 - NOT 81 or 91! 2) 'quatre-vingts' (80) has 's' but 'quatre-vingt-un' (81) loses it. 3) 'cents' plural: 'deux cents' (200) but 'deux cent un' (201). 4) 'mille' NEVER plural: 'trois mille' (3,000) not 'milles'. 5) Hyphens between all parts EXCEPT before/after 'et' or 'cent/mille'

title: Reference III: Jours et Mois
description: Days of the week, months, and seasons - never capitalized in French!

concepts.definition: Seven days - NEVER capitalized in French (unlike English!)
concepts.example: lundi (Monday), mardi (Tuesday), mercredi (Wednesday), jeudi (Thursday), vendredi (Friday), samedi (Saturday), dimanche (Sunday)

concepts.definition: Twelve months - also NEVER capitalized in French
concepts.example: janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre

concepts.definition: Four seasons - note the articles!
concepts.example: le printemps (spring), l'été (summer), l'automne (fall), l'hiver (winter)

concepts.definition: Essential words for talking about days and time
concepts.example: aujourd'hui (today), demain (tomorrow), hier (yesterday), cette semaine (this week), le week-end (the weekend)

title: Reference IV: Les Fêtes
description: French holidays and celebrations - from Bastille Day to crêpe day!

concepts.definition: France has 11 official public holidays - more than most countries!
concepts.example: le Nouvel An (Jan 1), Pâques (Easter), la Fête Nationale (July 14 - Bastille Day), Noël (Dec 25)

concepts.definition: July 14 - France's most important holiday celebrating the French Revolution (1789)
concepts.example: Military parade on Champs-Élysées, fireworks, parties - like July 4th in America but with more cheese!

concepts.definition: France is secular but many Catholic holidays are still official days off
concepts.example: Pâques (Easter), Ascension, Pentecôte (Pentecost), Assomption (Aug 15), Toussaint (Nov 1 - All Saints)

concepts.definition: France honors both world wars with official holidays
concepts.example: 8 mai - Victoire 1945 (WWII), 11 novembre - Armistice 1918 (WWI)

concepts.definition: Unique celebrations you won't find everywhere!
concepts.example: la Chandeleur (Feb 2 - Crêpe Day!), le Poisson d'Avril (April 1 - stick fish on backs!), la Fête de la Musique (June 21 - free concerts everywhere!)

concepts.definition: Two huge celebrations with fancy dinners called 'réveillons'
concepts.example: le Réveillon de Noël (Christmas Eve dinner), le Réveillon du Nouvel An (New Year's Eve), la Galette des Rois (Jan 6 - King Cake with hidden prize!)

concepts.definition: French Canada has unique celebrations
concepts.example: la Saint-Jean-Baptiste (June 24 - Quebec National Day), le Jour du Souvenir (Nov 11 - Remembrance Day)

concepts.definition: Essential phrases for celebrating
concepts.example: Joyeux Noël! (Merry Christmas!), Bonne année! (Happy New Year!), Joyeuses Pâques! (Happy Easter!), Bon anniversaire! (Happy Birthday!)

title: Reference V: Les Couleurs
description: Essential colors in French - learn how colors agree with nouns and create beautiful descriptions

concepts.definition: In French, colors are adjectives that agree with the noun in gender and number. They usually come AFTER the noun.
concepts.example: le ciel bleu (the blue sky), une maison blanche (a white house), des yeux verts (green eyes)

concepts.definition: The most common colors you'll use every day - memorize these first!
concepts.example: bleu (blue), rouge (red), vert (green), jaune (yellow), blanc (white), noir (black)

concepts.definition: Add -e to make most colors feminine. Some have special forms.
concepts.example: bleu → bleue, vert → verte, blanc → blanche, rouge → rouge (no change)

concepts.definition: Add -s for plural (unless already ends in -s or -x)
concepts.example: bleu → bleus (masculine plural), bleue → bleues (feminine plural), gris → gris (no change)

concepts.definition: Some colors never change: marron (brown), orange (orange). These are actually nouns used as adjectives!
concepts.example: un chat marron, une maison marron, des chats marron (no -s!)

concepts.definition: Colors with two words or modified colors are invariable (never change)
concepts.example: des yeux bleu clair (light blue eyes), des robes bleu foncé (dark blue dresses)

concepts.definition: Now you can ask about colors of things!
concepts.example: De quelle couleur est le ciel? (What color is the sky?) → Le ciel est bleu. Pourquoi est-ce que l'herbe est verte? (Why is grass green?)

title: Reference VI: La Francophonie
description: French-speaking countries around the world - 300 million speakers across 5 continents!

concepts.definition: French is spoken by 300+ million people across 29 countries as an official language
concepts.example: 5th most spoken language globally, 2nd most studied language, official language of UN, EU, NATO, Olympics

concepts.definition: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Monaco - 90 million French speakers
concepts.example: France (67M - birthplace), Belgium (11.5M - also Dutch/German), Switzerland (8.6M - also German/Italian), Luxembourg (632K), Monaco (39K)

concepts.definition: 8+ million French speakers, primarily in Quebec (Canada) and Haiti
concepts.example: Quebec (7.9M - 'Je me souviens'), Haiti (11.4M - French + Creole), Louisiana (200K speakers), Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon (6K)

concepts.definition: Africa has the MOST French speakers (60% of global total) and growing fast!
concepts.example: By 2050, 85% of French speakers will be in Africa. Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake France as #1 French-speaking country!

concepts.definition: 11 countries where French is the official language
concepts.example: Senegal (16M), Côte d'Ivoire (26M - economic hub), Mali (20M), Burkina Faso (21M), Niger (24M), Benin (12M), Togo (8M), Guinea (13M)

concepts.definition: French is the lingua franca connecting hundreds of ethnic groups
concepts.example: DRC (90M - 2nd largest!), Cameroon (27M - also English), Chad (16M), Congo-Brazzaville (5.5M), CAR (4.8M), Gabon (2.2M)

concepts.definition: French widely spoken alongside Arabic in former French colonies
concepts.example: Morocco (33% speak French), Algeria (33%), Tunisia (66%) - French used in business, education, media

concepts.definition: French official in 7 countries and island nations
concepts.example: Madagascar (28M), Rwanda (13M), Burundi (12M), Djibouti (990K), Comoros (870K), Seychelles (98K), Mauritius (1.3M)

concepts.definition: French departments and territories in the Caribbean
concepts.example: Guadeloupe (400K), Martinique (375K), French Guiana (290K) - all part of France with euros and French laws!

concepts.definition: Former French influence still present
concepts.example: Lebanon (40% speak French - Paris of Middle East), Vietnam (600K - legacy of French Indochina)

concepts.definition: French territories across the Pacific Ocean
concepts.example: French Polynesia/Tahiti (280K), New Caledonia (271K), Vanuatu (307K - French, English, Bislama official)

concepts.definition: By 2050, French will have 700 million speakers - mostly due to African population growth
concepts.example: DRC will have more French speakers than France! French will be Africa's most-spoken language. 85% of French speakers will be African.

title: Reference VII: Le Français en Chiffres
description: Fascinating statistics and linguistic facts about French - from phonemes to pangrams!

concepts.definition: French has 36-37 distinct sounds (phonemes) - 16 vowels and 20-21 consonants
concepts.example: 4 nasal vowels (ã, ẽ, õ, œ̃) - unique to French! No 'th' sound (why 'the' is hard). Uvular 'r' (back of throat).

concepts.definition: Each syllable gets equal time - unlike English which stresses certain words
concepts.example: French flows smoothly with even rhythm. No word stress like English! Emphasis on last syllable of phrases. Creates musical, flowing sound.

concepts.definition: French speakers talk fast! 7.0-8.0 syllables per second vs English 6.5
concepts.example: French needs more syllables to convey same info (lower information density), so speakers compensate by speaking faster!

concepts.definition: 26 letters + 5 diacritical marks + 2 ligatures
concepts.example: Letters: same as English. Accents: é è ê ë à ù û ç. Ligatures: œ (cœur), æ (rare). Total: 33 unique characters!

concepts.definition: 100,000 words in common use - educated speakers know 30,000 actively
concepts.example: Le Grand Robert dictionary: 100,000 words, 350,000 definitions. Average person: 5,000-30,000 words depending on education.

concepts.definition: 29% of English vocabulary comes from French (thanks to Norman Conquest 1066!)
concepts.example: 45% of English has Latin/French origins total. Beef, pork, royal, justice, parliament - all from French!

concepts.definition: 2 genders, 17-20 verb tenses, ~350 irregular verbs (only ~50 common)
concepts.example: Masculine/Feminine. 3 verb groups (-er, -ir, -re) + irregulars. ~25 'essential' irregular verbs to memorize. SVO word order like English.

concepts.definition: 5th most spoken, 2nd most studied, 3rd language of business
concepts.example: 300M speakers (2023), projected 700M by 2050. Official in 29 countries. One of 6 UN languages. Growing fast in Africa!

concepts.definition: Quirky and interesting trivia about French
concepts.example: Longest word: 'anticonstitutionnellement' (25 letters). Most common word: 'de'. Most common letter: 'e' (15%). No word for 'home' or 'shallow'!

concepts.definition: Words link together smoothly - consonants connect to following vowels
concepts.example: 'les enfants' sounds like 'lay-zahn-fahn' (z sound links). 'un homme' = 'uh-nom'. Creates beautiful flowing speech!

concepts.definition: Official authority on French language since 1635 - protects 'purity' of French
concepts.example: 40 immortals (lifetime members) decide official French. Resist English words. Prefer 'ordinateur' to 'computer', 'courriel' to 'email'.

concepts.definition: A sentence using all 26 letters
concepts.example: 'Portez ce vieux whisky au juge blond qui fume' (Bring this old whisky to the blonde judge who smokes)
